summary: FireCalendar India turns 25 years of NASA FIRMS satellite fire detections into one consistent burning calendar for any area in India. MODIS (2000 onward) and VIIRS (2012 onward) count fires differently: VIIRS's finer 375 m pixels see about six times more fire activity, so joining the records naively creates a false jump in 2012. We count "fire cell-days" on an equal-area H3 grid and calibrate MODIS into VIIRS units with factors fitted per region, month and day/night pass over the 2012–2025 overlap, each with a 90% uncertainty interval. The false 2012 jump shrinks from 4.6× to 1.08×, and held-out tests predict monthly totals within 16.7% (bias −1.2%). Our web app lets anyone draw an area or pick a preset and instantly see a month-by-year calendar, anomalies against the usual, the typical fire season and any month's fires on the map, with CSV downloads. Fire managers, scientists and air-quality agencies can now tell at a glance whether this month is unusual, on a record that continues as MODIS retires.
details:
What it does
FireCalendar India turns 25 years of NASA satellite fire detections into one consistent burning calendar for any area in India. A user picks a preset region (such as Punjab or Odisha), draws an area on the map, or enters a point and radius, then presses Analyze. They get:

A burning calendar: years down, months across, with the harmonized fire activity printed in every cell.
An anomaly view: each month compared with the same month in other years, labelled "unusually high" or "unusually low".
A plain-language verdict, for example "Punjab, December 2025: 57% below a typical December. Fire season usually runs September to December."
Fires on the map: click any month in the calendar to see that month's real detections, such as 51,527 fires in Punjab in November 2016.
Charts of the typical year, year-to-date and annual totals, with a raw vs harmonized toggle that shows the false 2012 jump disappearing.
CSV downloads of hotspots and the calendar, PNG downloads of every chart, and a table view of every chart.
How it works

Data: NASA FIRMS active fires for India. MODIS Terra and Aqua (MCD14ML, 2000–2025), VIIRS Suomi NPP (VNP14IMG, 2012–2025), VIIRS NOAA-20 (VJ114IMG, 2024 onward) and the FIRMS API for 2026.
Filtering: vegetation fires only; MODIS confidence 30 or higher, VIIRS nominal or high.
Gridding: every detection goes into an H3 hexagon cell of about 5 km². Our unit is the "fire cell-day" (a cell that burned on a given day counts once), which removes most of the pixel-size difference between the 1 km and 375 m sensors.
Calibration: Aqua MODIS and Suomi NPP VIIRS pass overhead at the same local time (13:30 and 01:30). For every 2° region, calendar month and day/night pass, we fit a factor k = VIIRS ÷ MODIS over the 2012–2025 overlap. Sparse regions are pulled toward the national factor, and a bootstrap over years gives each factor a 90% uncertainty interval. Terra and NOAA-20 are chained in with their own ratios.
Validation: fitted on 2012–2018 and tested on 2019–2025, monthly totals for India are predicted within 16.7% (bias −1.2%), against 29.1% for a single constant. The false 2012 jump falls from 4.6× to 1.08×.
Benefits and intended impact

One consistent record from 2000 to today, already in VIIRS units, so it keeps going after MODIS retires.
It answers the question fire and disaster managers actually ask, "Is this month unusual for this place?", for any custom area, not only fixed administrative regions.
It helps air-quality and land managers track seasonal burning, such as Punjab's October–November paddy-residue fires, year by year.
It gives scientists a reproducible, harmonized series, with raw counts and calibration factors kept alongside.
Our aim is an early-warning view: unusual months stand out instantly, and preparation can be timed to each area's fire season. The same method can extend to the whole world.
Tools and languages

Data pipeline: Python, DuckDB with the H3 extension, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib.
API: FastAPI with DuckDB querying compact Parquet files.
Web app: React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL, Terra Draw, Observable Plot, Turf.
Hosting: Render (API and static site), plus a GitHub Actions keep-warm ping.
No special hardware; everything runs on free-tier cloud services.
How it is creative

Instead of matching individual pixels, we change the unit of counting to fire cell-days on an equal-area grid, so two very different sensors become comparable.
Calibration is local: by region, month and day/night, with honest uncertainty shown as whiskers on the chart.
The results are written in plain language as well as charts, so non-specialists understand them at once.
A calendar month links straight to the actual fires on the map, connecting the statistics to what the satellites saw.
An "exploded view" illustration shows the whole method as stacked layers: MODIS, VIIRS, grid, calibration, calendar.
Factors we considered

Scientific fairness: comparing only same-time overpasses, keeping raw data
